What should an Oklahoma City homeowner know before selling?

Oklahoma City is large enough that selling a house depends on which part of it you are in, which county bills the property and which school district the address falls in. A seller can list, sell privately or take a cash offer, and this page walks through the local facts that shape each choice.

How big is Oklahoma City and which counties does it cover?

Oklahoma City covers 620.79 square miles, of which 601.11 is land, and it is the county seat of Oklahoma County. Its limits also reach into Canadian, Cleveland and Pottawatomie counties, though the parts outside Oklahoma County are mostly suburban or rural watershed land. The 2020 census counted 681,054 residents.

Because the city crosses county lines, the tax bill for a house depends on the county where it sits. Most addresses are billed by the Oklahoma County Treasurer, but a house in the southern edge may be billed by Cleveland County. Check the parcel before you plan closing figures.

How is Oklahoma City laid out?

The city is split by the North Canadian River, renamed the Oklahoma River inside city limits in 2004. North and south sides have a different character, according to Wikipedia: the north has urban neighborhoods near the center and sprawling suburbs further out, while the south is more industrial and grew up around the Stockyards and meatpacking plants.

The city also has three large lakes, Hefner and Overholser in the northwest and Stanley Draper in the far southeast. Downtown had about 7,600 residents in the Wikipedia count, and the city lies in the Sandstone Hills with Cross Timbers terrain in the northeast. A buyer for a south side bungalow and a buyer for a north side suburban house are usually different people, so pricing and marketing differ.

What is Oklahoma City's history in brief?

Oklahoma City was founded in the Land Run of 1889 and grew to more than 10,000 people within hours. The April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building killed 168 people.

The oil bust that followed the 1982 Penn Square Bank collapse hit the city's housing market hard, as Wikipedia describes it, and downtown has been rebuilt since through public projects. The point for sellers: Oklahoma City real estate has gone through sharp cycles tied to energy prices, so ask for current local sales data rather than relying on old rules of thumb.

Who are the major employers in Oklahoma City?

The State of Oklahoma is the largest, followed by Tinker Air Force Base. The list below is from Wikipedia's March 2024 table of top employers:

Devon Energy and Expand Energy, both Fortune 500 companies, are headquartered here. Tinker, in the southeast, is described as the largest military air depot in the nation. Job transfers to and from these employers are a common reason for a fast sale, since a move date can be set by an employer, not the housing market.

What does Oklahoma City weather mean for a house?

Severe weather season runs from March through June, especially April and May, and the city has been struck by about 150 tornadoes since 1890 along with hail and occasional derechoes. Wikipedia counts 13 violent tornadoes in the city's record. Annual precipitation is about 35.9 inches and temperatures reach 100 degrees on about 10.4 days a year.

Wikipedia also notes that droughts and flash flooding both occur regularly. A buyer's inspector will concentrate on:

  • Roof age and hail damage
  • Storm shelter or safe room condition
  • Foundation movement after dry spells and heavy rain
  • Drainage and creek or floodplain proximity

The city runs a Storm Shelter Registry where residents can register a shelter's address, type and location to help first responders. Registering a shelter and keeping its permit record is useful documentation at sale.

What code rules can affect an Oklahoma City sale?

Oklahoma City code enforcement acts on complaints. An inspector visits, issues a notice, and enforcement follows if the problem is not fixed by the next visit. For overgrown lots and junk the city can clean up and bill the owner, and for exterior maintenance violations it can write citations.

Common rules sellers should check before listing:

  • Grass is a violation at 12 inches, and owners must maintain adjacent alleys and right-of-way.
  • Vehicles that are inoperable, wrecked or junked are a public nuisance after 72 hours.
  • Parking on an unpaved surface or sidewalk, including boats, trailers and RVs, is a violation.
  • Roofs, fences and painted surfaces must be kept in good repair.
  • Dilapidated and unsecured structures, with damaged foundations or open doors and windows, violate state law as well as city code.
  • Bulk waste may go to the curb no more than three days before pickup.

The county treasurer's office notes that special assessments for weeds, cleaning, paving and nuisance abatement are certified to the treasurer after they become delinquent and are placed as a lien on the property account. That lien can show up in a title search. See the city's code enforcement page.

How do property taxes work for an Oklahoma County home?

The Oklahoma County Assessor sets values and the Treasurer collects the bill. Taxes can be paid in full or in two installments, with the first half or the full amount due by December 31. If nothing is paid by then, the whole amount becomes delinquent on January 1, and if half is paid the rest is due March 31.

Interest on delinquent payments is 18 percent a year, added at 1.5 percent monthly on the 15th, and a missing statement is not a legal reason to waive it. The Treasurer says assessments are certified to its office on October 1, and a new owner should give the assessor a correct mailing address before September 30. Mortgage servicers often pay through a third-party tax service, so a payment can take time to appear online.

When a house sells, the closing agent normally prorates the current year's tax and pays any unpaid balance from the seller's proceeds. Look up your account on the county's public access search before you list.

How do you get around Oklahoma City?

Interstates 35, 40 and 44 pass through the city, with I-235 and I-240 as connectors. The stretch of I-44 between NW 23rd and NW 36th Streets carried about 167,200 vehicles a day in 2018, the busiest road in the state. Will Rogers World Airport served 4,341,159 passengers in 2018, and Amtrak stops at the Santa Fe Depot downtown.

Commute time matters to buyers, so a house near an interstate ramp or the Kilpatrick Turnpike has a different appeal than one far from the highway grid.

Which school districts serve Oklahoma City addresses?

Oklahoma City Public Schools covers the largest part of the city, but many other districts overlap it. In Oklahoma County Wikipedia lists Putnam City, Western Heights, Mid-Del, Moore, Edmond, Deer Creek, Mustang, Harrah, Choctaw/Nicoma Park and others. Districts in Cleveland County covering part of the city include Moore and Little Axe.

A single Oklahoma City mailing address can sit in any of these, so confirm the district from the county records or the school district's boundary tool.

What do Oklahoma City sellers usually run into?

  • Hail or storm damage with an open or denied insurance claim
  • Inherited houses in older neighborhoods where heirs are out of state
  • Rental houses with deferred maintenance or an open code notice
  • Vacant houses that attract weed, junk or unsecured-structure complaints
  • Owners facing a job relocation or a mortgage problem

A cash buyer typically purchases a house in its current condition and covers the closing paperwork the buyer handles. Compare any offer with what a listing would net after repairs, fees and time on the market, and ask for the terms in writing before agreeing.

More questions about Oklahoma City, OK

Is Oklahoma City in more than one county?

Yes. The city is the county seat of Oklahoma County, and its limits extend into Canadian, Cleveland and Pottawatomie counties. The county that bills the house depends on where the parcel sits.

When are Oklahoma County property taxes due?

The first half or the full amount is due by December 31. If nothing is paid by then, the whole amount is delinquent January 1, and if half is paid the rest is due March 31.

What interest rate applies to late property tax in Oklahoma County?

The Treasurer charges 18 percent a year on delinquent payments, added monthly at 1.5 percent on the 15th. Not receiving a statement does not waive the interest.

How high can grass be in Oklahoma City before it is a violation?

City ordinance treats grass as a violation at 12 inches. Owners are also responsible for alleys and right-of-way next to their property, and the city can clean up and bill the owner.

Can I sell an Oklahoma City house with code violations or storm damage?

Yes. Cash buyers purchase houses in their present condition, though open code notices or liens may need to be handled at closing. Get the terms in writing before you decide.

What should a Norman homeowner know before selling?

Norman is a university city of roughly 131,000 people where the sale of a house is shaped by three things: the University of Oklahoma, the city's large footprint, and Cleveland County's tax and recording offices. A seller here can list the house, sell it privately, or take a cash offer, and each route works differently depending on the condition of the property and how soon the money is needed.

This page covers the city first and then the local steps that tend to matter at closing.

How big is Norman and where does it sit?

Norman is a large, spread-out city. The 2010 figures show 189.42 square miles of total area, 178.77 of them land, and the city center is about 20 miles from the center of Oklahoma City, with Moore lying between the two.

The land changes from west to east. The western side is prairie, while the east around Lake Thunderbird holds roughly 6,000 acres of lakes and Cross Timbers forest. Elevation is close to 1,171 feet. A house on the west side and a house near the lake can have very different yards, drainage and tree cover, even though both carry a Norman address.

How did Norman start?

Norman was founded in the Land Run of April 22, 1889, and incorporated on May 13, 1891. The name comes from Abner Ernest Norman, a 23-year-old surveyor whose crew carved "Norman's Camp" on an elm tree near what is now Classen Boulevard and Lindsey Street.

Two local businessmen lobbied the territorial government for a university, and on December 19, 1890 the council passed the bill that created the University of Oklahoma in Norman, about 17 years before statehood. The completion of Interstate 35 in June 1959 turned Norman into a commuter city for Oklahoma City: the population was 33,412 in 1960 and 52,117 ten years later.

What are Norman's neighborhoods like?

Norman has several well-defined areas, and the right buyer pool differs for each. Wikipedia's neighborhood notes describe a few of them:

  • Downtown, about 2 square miles bounded by University Boulevard, Symmes Street, Porter Avenue and Daws Street, with some of the oldest buildings in Oklahoma.
  • Hall Park, northeast of downtown, annexed in 2005 and advertised in the early 1960s as the first "all-electric town" in the United States.
  • The campus area, with neo-Gothic and Queen Anne style houses and churches.
  • The Miller Historic District and the Chautauqua Historic District, both city-designated preservation districts.

If your house is in a historic district, ask the city's planning staff before doing exterior work, since preservation rules can apply to windows, siding and additions.

Who employs people in Norman, and how does that touch a home sale?

The University of Oklahoma is the largest employer by a wide margin. Norman's 2022 annual financial report, as reproduced on Wikipedia, lists the top employers this way:

Enrollment at the university is about 30,000, per the same article. A school calendar affects timing: houses near campus may turn over around the academic year, and landlords who own rentals near campus may want a sale that does not depend on a tenant's lease end date. The National Weather Center, which houses NOAA and university weather research, is also a significant employer in town.

What is Norman's weather and what does it do to a house?

Norman has a humid subtropical climate with average annual precipitation near 38 inches. May and June are the wettest months, and July daytime highs average about 92.5 degrees Fahrenheit.

Tornado season peaks from March through June. Wikipedia notes a high-end EF2 tornado on the southeast side of the city on the night of February 26, 2023, and tornado events in Cleveland County on May 10, 2010 that destroyed homes and businesses inside the city limits. A buyer's inspector will pay attention to roof age, hail damage and any storm shelter. Keep repair receipts and insurance paperwork ready.

How do I get around Norman and the metro?

Norman is a car-based city. About 80 percent of residents drive alone to work, per the Wikipedia figure, and Interstate 35 carried more than 99,000 vehicles a day in 2007. State Highway 9 and U.S. 77 are the other main routes.

Embark provides fare-free bus and paratransit service across the Norman area, with express service to downtown Oklahoma City. Amtrak's Heartland Flyer stops at the Norman Depot with daily round trips to Oklahoma City and Fort Worth. Will Rogers World Airport is about 20 miles northwest. These details help in a listing description and in answering a buyer's commute questions.

What permits and codes apply in Norman?

Norman adopted updated building, fire and property maintenance codes effective June 22, 2023. The list includes the 2018 International Building, Residential, Existing Building, Plumbing and Property Maintenance codes, the 2018 Fuel Gas Code and the 2020 National Electrical Code, with state and local amendments.

Permits and inspections are handled by the Development Services Division at 225 N. Webster Avenue. Its checklist for one and two family construction includes new homes, additions, alterations, storm shelters and storage buildings, so a garage shelter or backyard shed may have a permit file. Reviewing that record before listing can prevent a surprise from a buyer's lender. The city's building codes page lists the adopted codes.

What Oklahoma transfer tax applies when a Norman house sells?

Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax on deeds. The rate is 75 cents for each $500 of the price or any part of $500, and the tax applies when the price exceeds $100.

At that rate a $200,000 sale needs 400 units of $0.75, or $300 in stamps. The county clerk sells and affixes the stamps when the deed is filed, and the Oklahoma Tax Commission says either side of the deed can be held responsible, so the contract should say who pays. Deeds between related people without payment and deeds to a person's own revocable trust are among the listed exemptions in 68 O.S. section 3202.

On the property tax side, Cleveland County says half the bill is due by December 31 and the second half by March 31.

Which school districts cover Norman?

Norman Public Schools is the largest, with 15 elementary schools, four middle schools and two high schools and more than 17,000 students, per Wikipedia. Noble Public Schools serves southeastern parts of Norman and Little Axe serves the east, while parts of the city fall in McLoud, Mid-Del, Moore and Robin Hill districts.

Because several districts overlap the city, the district for a given address should be confirmed rather than assumed.

What do Norman sellers usually run into?

  • Student rentals with worn finishes or a lease that overlaps the sale
  • Inherited houses where heirs live out of state
  • Storm damage that was never fully repaired
  • Older homes near campus with outdated wiring or plumbing
  • Sellers who need to close fast because of a job transfer or financial strain

A cash buyer will usually look at the house as it stands, which lets the seller skip repairs and showings. Get the offer in writing, ask what the buyer pays for, and compare it with a listed sale after fees and carrying costs.

When are Cleveland County property taxes due?

Taxes may be paid in full or in two halves. At least half must be paid by December 31, and the second half is due by March 31, according to Cleveland County.

Which building codes does Norman use?

The city adopted its 2018 International Codes and the 2020 National Electrical Code with local amendments, effective June 22, 2023. Permits and inspections are handled by Development Services at 225 N. Webster Avenue.

How big is Broken Arrow and where does it sit?

Broken Arrow covers about 45 square miles in the northeast corner of Oklahoma, in the region known as Green Country, and the 2020 census counted 113,540 residents. That made it the fourth most populous city in the state and a major part of the Tulsa metropolitan area, which had 1,023,988 residents.

Most of the city is in Tulsa County, and areas that extend into Wagoner County are zoned to Broken Arrow Public Schools. The size matters for sellers: a house near the downtown Main Street area, one by the Creek Turnpike on the south side and one on the Wagoner County edge sit in different pockets with different commutes and different county offices.

Green Country is described as the most topographically diverse part of Oklahoma, with hills and lakes, so lots can slope or sit near creeks more than the flat plains image suggests.

What is the history behind the Broken Arrow name?

The name comes from a Creek community in Alabama. After removal along the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, Creek families founded a new settlement in Indian Territory and kept the name, which is Rekackv in the Muscogee language and means broken arrow.

The present townsite dates to 1902, when the Missouri-Kansas-Texas Railroad was granted townsite rights and William S. Fears of the Arkansas Valley Town Site Company chose the location about 18 miles southeast of Tulsa. The line was finished in 1903 and still runs through the middle of the city, now owned by Union Pacific for freight.

Farming and strip coal mining drove the early economy. The city stayed small until the 1960s, when the Broken Arrow Expressway, State Highway 51, linked it to downtown Tulsa. Population went from a little above 11,000 in 1970 to more than 50,000 in 1990 and over 74,000 by 2000. That timeline explains why so much of the housing stock dates from the 1970s onward.

What do Broken Arrow employers and colleges add to the housing market?

Broken Arrow has the third-largest concentration of manufacturers in Oklahoma, even though it grew as a bedroom community for Tulsa workers. City leaders have pushed for more local jobs and shopping so residents spend less time commuting elsewhere.

Education institutions also anchor the area:

  • Northeastern State University's Broken Arrow campus, opened in 2001, with about 3,000 upperclass and graduate students.
  • Tulsa Technology Center's Broken Arrow campus, established in 1983, with about 3,500 secondary and adult students.
  • Rhema Bible Training Center, founded in 1974 on 110 acres.

A house that needs updates can be hard to sell on the open market, since retail buyers often ask for repairs before closing.

Which school districts serve Broken Arrow addresses?

Broken Arrow is served by three districts: Broken Arrow Public Schools, Union Public Schools and Bixby Public Schools. Within Tulsa County, most of the city is in Broken Arrow Public Schools, the northwestern area is in Union, and a far southwest area is in Bixby.

Because the boundaries cut through the city, two similar houses a few blocks apart can feed different schools. Buyers and their agents check this early, so it is useful to know your district and say so in any conversation about the house.

How do Broken Arrow roads and transit affect a sale?

State Highway 51, the Broken Arrow Expressway, crosses the north side of the city and leads northwest to downtown Tulsa. Heading east, it connects to the Muskogee Turnpike, and the Creek Turnpike curves around the south side, linking the Turner Turnpike with the Will Rogers Turnpike.

Tulsa Transit runs one route between Broken Arrow and Tulsa on weekdays. Most households rely on cars, so proximity to an expressway or turnpike entrance is a common selling point and a house beside a busy road is a common objection.

Hot summers and freezing winters mean cooling systems and pipes do the heaviest work, and a buyer's inspector will test both.

How does Broken Arrow handle permits and building codes?

The City of Broken Arrow's Inspections division checks that new structures and modifications meet adopted codes, inspects every phase of construction, issues certificates of occupancy and investigates alleged violations. It also addresses unsafe or unsanitary buildings that endanger occupants or the neighborhood.

The city has adopted the 2024 international residential, building, fire, mechanical and fuel gas codes and the 2023 National Electric Code, each as amended by the state and by the city. Inspection scheduling goes through the city's online self-service portal.

If you finished a garage, added a bedroom or replaced a furnace, locate the permit and sign-off. Open or missing records can slow a conventional buyer's financing, while a direct buyer will usually discuss the house as it stands.

What should a Broken Arrow seller know about city utility billing?

The City of Broken Arrow bills water, sanitary sewer, curbside trash, stormwater, streetlight and LifeRide on one monthly statement, and customers can manage the account through its Water Smart portal. New residential customers pay a refundable $100 deposit, which can be waived after a favorable credit check, and a non-refundable $30 start or transfer fee.

Bills are due no earlier than 20 days after the billing date, and a 10 percent late fee applies after 5:00 p.m. on the day after the due date. Gas comes from Oklahoma Natural Gas and electric from Public Service Company of Oklahoma.

When you sell, schedule a stop or transfer in Water Smart so your final bill closes on the sale date. Unpaid city charges can become a closing headache.

How is Broken Arrow property tax set in Tulsa County?

The Tulsa County Assessor values each Broken Arrow property as of January 1 and revalues residential property every year. The valuation notice gives you 30 calendar days to protest in writing, and an informal protest can happen by phone.

Assessed value is 11 percent of taxable fair cash value. Taxable value is capped at a 5 percent yearly rise, or 3 percent with a homestead, but the cap is removed when the property is purchased. A new owner therefore sees a bigger bill than the previous one, which the assessor lists among its common questions.

Homestead applications are due by March 15 or within 30 days of the increase notice to count for the current year. The assessor also notes you owe the whole year's bill on a property as it stood on January 1, even if you sell part of it later.

What does Oklahoma require at a Broken Arrow closing?

The documentary stamp tax is 75 cents per $500 of consideration under 68 O.S. section 3201, and the clerk affixes it when the deed is filed. A $320,000 sale involves 640 units, or $480.

Oklahoma sellers of one- and two-family homes must provide the buyer a written condition disclosure or a disclaimer statement under 60 O.S. section 833. Exempt transfers, such as gifts without consideration, need the exemption noted on the deed.

More questions about Broken Arrow, OK

Is Broken Arrow in Tulsa County?

Mostly. The city is in Tulsa County, with a portion that extends into Wagoner County. Your tax notice shows which county assessor and clerk handle the property.

Which school district is my Broken Arrow house in?

It depends on the address. Most Tulsa County addresses are in Broken Arrow Public Schools, the northwest corner is in Union and a far southwest area is in Bixby.

What deposit does Broken Arrow charge for new utility service?

The city's page lists a refundable $100 deposit for new residential customers, plus a $30 non-refundable start or transfer fee. Contact Utility Billing at 116 E Dallas Street for specifics.

Does the Tulsa County cap on taxable value apply after I sell?

No. The assessor says the statutory cap is removed when a property is purchased, so the buyer's taxable value can reset to current market value.

Can I sell a Broken Arrow house without making repairs?

Yes. Many direct buyers purchase as-is. You still owe the written disclosure or disclaimer statement under Oklahoma law.

Where is Edmond and how did it start?

Edmond is a city in Oklahoma County that borders the northern edge of Oklahoma City, and it is the fifth most populous city in the state. The 2020 census counted 94,428 residents, up from 81,405 in 2010 and 68,315 in 2000.

The Santa Fe Railroad built a water and coaling station here in 1887, on the highest point of the line in Oklahoma County, and named it for freight agent Edmond Burdick. The town sprang up on April 22, 1889, during the Land Run, and the first public schoolhouse in Oklahoma Territory was completed that August. It still stands on 2nd Street and opens to visitors on the first two Saturdays of each month.

In 1890 the territorial legislature placed a teaching school in Edmond, which became the University of Central Oklahoma. The city has grown in every census since, and a seller should expect neighborhoods from several eras, from early plats near downtown to subdivisions built after the 1970s.

What weather risks should an Edmond seller expect?

Edmond sits in Tornado Alley and in the Cross Timbers region, so tornadoes, hail, ice storms and drought are all part of the picture. Wikipedia's climate summary adds that prolonged droughts often lead to wildfires and heavy rain to flash flooding, and that severe ice and snowstorms happen sporadically.

For a house, that translates into:

  • Roof age and hail damage, which inspectors and insurers check first.
  • Soil shifting during drought and wet cycles, which can crack slabs and brick.
  • Tree damage from ice storms, particularly on lots with mature post oak and blackjack oak.

Edmond lies in the Sandstone Hills, which are known for hills and those oak species, and Arcadia Lake and Twin Bridges Lake are on its east side. Keep roof and insurance claim records handy when you talk with any buyer, since storm history is one of the first things they ask about.

How do Edmond utilities and city services work?

Edmond provides electric, water, sewer, trash and stormwater services through city departments, and the Utility Customer Service office bills all of them. Edmond Electric describes itself as Oklahoma's largest community-owned electric utility, serving the community since 1908 and more than 90,000 residents inside city limits.

Having one municipal bill makes moving simpler: you arrange a final read and the buyer opens a new account. Ask the city about any outstanding balance so it does not attach to the sale.

The city's Community Image program covers code enforcement. It identifies violations of Edmond ordinances and state law inside city limits, notifies the responsible party and looks for voluntary compliance. Resolve any open notice before you list, since a buyer's title company or lender may ask about it.

Which building rules apply to Edmond houses?

Edmond's Building and Fire Code Services department publishes the codes it follows. Its page says that as of August 14, 2023, the city adopted the 2018 International Code Council family of codes for permits applied for or issued on or after that date, consistent with the minimum codes set by the state's Uniform Building Code Commission.

Check the current page for later changes. For a seller, the practical point is the permit history: a remodel, an addition or a new roof should have a permit and a final inspection. Missing paperwork can stall an appraisal or an inspection response, though many cash buyers will take a house as is.

How do Edmond schools and transit shape buyer interest?

Most of Edmond is in Edmond Public Schools, which operates three comprehensive high schools: Edmond Memorial, Edmond North and Edmond Santa Fe, as well as Boulevard Academy. Portions fall in Deer Creek, Jones and Luther districts, so verify the district for your address.

Interstate 35 and US 77 run through the city, and Citylink Edmond provides public bus service. The University of Central Oklahoma and Oklahoma Christian University are both in the city. Because school assignment drives many buyers' searches, put the correct district up front in any conversation about the house.

How are Edmond properties assessed and appealed in Oklahoma County?

The Oklahoma County Assessor values property and mails a Notice of Valuation, and the owner has 30 days from the mailing date to file a written protest. The assessor then schedules an informal hearing and issues a written decision within 7 calendar days.

If you disagree, you have 15 calendar days from the decision's mailing date to appeal to the county Board of Equalization. Oklahoma's statewide rules say protest proceedings must be finished by May 31 or the Board's adjournment date. The county's own pages say the Board sits from the fourth Monday in January through May 31 for business personal property.

Oklahoma assesses real property as of January 1, so the owner on that date is the one who may protest the current year's value. If you sell during the year, settle the proration with the buyer at closing.

What does Oklahoma require for an Edmond deed and disclosure?

The state's documentary stamp tax is 75 cents on each $500 of the price or part of it. On a $425,000 sale the tax is $637.50, paid at the county clerk when the deed is recorded, and it is not paid until stamps are affixed.

Title 60 section 833 requires sellers of one- or two-unit homes to deliver either a disclosure statement or a disclaimer statement. Deeds between spouses or from parents to children without payment are generally exempt, with the exemption noted on the deed.

Is Edmond in Oklahoma County?

Yes. Edmond is a city in Oklahoma County, on the northern border of Oklahoma City. The Oklahoma County Assessor and County Clerk handle valuation and recording.

How long do I have to protest my Oklahoma County valuation?

You have 30 days from the date the Notice of Valuation was mailed to file a written protest with the Oklahoma County Assessor. The informal hearing decision follows within 7 calendar days.

Who provides electricity in Edmond?

Edmond Electric, a city-owned utility, provides electric service inside city limits. The city also bills water, sewer, trash and stormwater through its Utility Customer Service office.

Do hail and tornadoes affect selling an Edmond house?

They can. Edmond is in Tornado Alley, so buyers and insurers look at roof age, hail history and storm repairs. Gather claim paperwork and roof records before you accept offers.

What documentary stamp tax applies to an Edmond sale?

Oklahoma charges 75 cents per $500 of consideration when the deed is filed. A $300,000 price means 600 units, or $450.

Where is Lawton and what is it known for?

Lawton is the county seat of Comanche County in southwestern Oklahoma, about 87 miles southwest of Oklahoma City. At 90,381 people in the 2020 census it is the sixth-largest city in the state and the largest in western Oklahoma.

The land is flat to gently rolling, and the Wichita Mountains rise north of the city, with Mount Scott and Mount Pinchot among the highest points. Interstate 44, which is the H. E. Bailey Turnpike here, runs through along with U.S. 62, U.S. 277, U.S. 281 and State Highway 7. Lawton-Fort Sill Regional Airport, Greyhound and the Lawton Area Transit System provide other ways in and out.

The Comanche Nation is headquartered in the city, and Lawton was built on former reservation land of the Kiowa, Comanche and Apache peoples.

How did Lawton start?

Lawton opened to settlement through a lottery and auction. President McKinley's proclamation of July 4, 1901 put about 2,000,000 acres of land the government called surplus under federal control. Lots in the new town were auctioned beginning August 6, 1901, over about 60 days.

The city is named for Major General Henry Ware Lawton, a Medal of Honor recipient killed in the Philippine-American War. Fort Sill had been established earlier, in 1869, and the two have been linked since. The city's Downtown I Urban Renewal Plan says code enforcement should be encouraged to preserve existing property and protect it from blighting influences, which is worth knowing if your house is near downtown.

What does Fort Sill mean for Lawton homes?

Fort Sill is Lawton's largest employer, with more than 5,000 full-time employees according to Wikipedia, and the Fort Sill Joint Land Use Study puts its regional impact near $2 billion a year. The base trains more than 18,000 Army recruits a year in a 10-week basic course and runs artillery, rocket and aviation training.

That activity affects houses. The land use study notes that aircraft noise from Henry Post Army Airfield reaches the northern part of Lawton, that range noise extends off the installation, and that heavy artillery vibration is felt along the north-northeastern boundary. Sellers near the base should expect buyers to ask about noise. Be direct about what is audible.

Training courses and unit moves bring people in and out of town, so some Lawton owners sell on a timeline set by orders or by a rental that ended. A house that needs work after a tenant leaves is one reason owners skip the listing process.

  • Goodyear Tire and Rubber: about 2,400 full-time employees
  • Others named: Lawton Public Schools, Comanche County Memorial Hospital, Southwestern Hospital, the City of Lawton, Cameron University and Bar S Foods

How hot, dry and stormy is Lawton, and what does that do to a roof?

Lawton has a relatively dry humid subtropical climate and sits in Tornado Alley. It averages 31 days a year at or above 100 degrees Fahrenheit, eight days that stay below freezing, about 31.6 inches of precipitation and under 3 inches of snow.

Triple-digit heat is hard on roofing, siding and cooling systems, and tornado season adds storm risk. Buyers commonly ask for roof age and any insurance claim history, so keep invoices and claim letters in one folder.

Which school districts and colleges serve Lawton?

Lawton Public Schools is the main district, with two prekindergarten centers, 24 elementary schools, three middle schools and three high schools: Eisenhower, Lawton and MacArthur. Bishop, Flower Mound, Cache and Geronimo operate separate districts around the city.

Higher education includes Cameron University, which enrolled nearly 3,700 students in 2024, Comanche Nation College and the Great Plains Technology Center. Private options include Trinity Christian Academy, Lawton Academy of Arts and Science and Lawton Christian School. A house on the edge of town may fall in one of the neighboring districts, so check the address before quoting a school.

What city code issues affect sellers in Lawton?

Weeds or grass over 12 inches high violate the Lawton city code, and failing to keep a property below that height can lead to a court citation. In 2024 the City Council also passed Ordinance 24-1810 on vacant lots, so owners should check the rules before they close or leave a lot unattended.

As reported by the Southwest Ledger, after the city cleans up out-of-compliance bulk waste or mows a property, it sends an itemized bill. The owner has 10 days to appeal to the Director of Community Services, a hearing follows within 10 days, and the owner has 30 days to pay before the city files a lien with the Comanche County Clerk. Reported fines run up to $300 for a first violation, $500 for a second within a year and $750 for later ones.

  • Mow and clear the property before showings.
  • Remove bulk waste according to the city's Solid Waste guidelines.
  • Open any city bill promptly, since the 10-day appeal clock starts on receipt.
  • Search the Lawton Code of Ordinances on Municode for the section that applies to your address.

When are Comanche County property taxes due?

Oklahoma property tax is due on November 1 each year, and the county treasurer collects it for schools, the city, the county and other districts. State law lets owners pay half before January 1 and the rest before April 1, and a missed first half makes the full amount delinquent.

The Comanche County Assessor lists and maintains records on all taxable property, helps with homestead filings, answers valuation protests and appears before the County Board of Equalization. The office is at 315 SW 5th Street, Room 301, Lawton, and the phone number is 580-355-1052. As elsewhere in Oklahoma, homestead applications are generally due by March 15, so confirm the date with the office.

At closing, a title company usually confirms the treasurer's balance. If you sell in the spring and the second half is not yet paid, expect that to be split at the table or paid off from proceeds.

What should a Lawton seller do first?

First decide whether time or price matters more. A listing may reach a financed buyer, and military buyers may be in that pool, but it adds showings, inspections and a lender timeline. A direct cash purchase gives a shorter path when the house needs work, has tenants or belongs to an estate.

Oklahoma requires a seller to give the buyer a disclaimer or disclosure statement before an offer is accepted (60 O.S. section 833). Gather permits, repair receipts and tax statements first, then call us about the Lawton address. We explain what a cash offer would cover, and you decide whether to accept.

How big is Lawton compared with other Oklahoma cities?

Lawton had 90,381 residents in the 2020 census, which makes it the sixth-largest city in Oklahoma and the largest in western Oklahoma.

Does Fort Sill noise affect Lawton house sales?

It can. The Fort Sill Joint Land Use Study says aircraft noise reaches the northern part of Lawton and range noise extends off the base in every direction. Sellers should answer buyer questions honestly.

What is the weed height rule in Lawton?

Weeds or grass above 12 inches violate the city code, and the city can issue a court citation. Cleanup and mowing costs billed by the city can become a lien if unpaid after 30 days.

Who values property in Comanche County?

The Comanche County Assessor, at 315 SW 5th Street, Room 301 in Lawton (580-355-1052). The Treasurer collects the tax, and valuation disputes go to the Assessor and then the County Board of Equalization.

Do I have to disclose problems when selling a house in Oklahoma?

Yes. You must deliver either a disclaimer statement or a condition disclosure statement before the buyer's offer is accepted, under 60 O.S. section 833.

How does selling a house in Moore, Oklahoma work?

A Moore homeowner can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer, and the choice mostly turns on how much time the house needs and what shape it is in. Moore is a separate city, not part of Oklahoma City, even though Oklahoma City wraps around it on three sides. That matters for paperwork, because permits, code complaints and utility accounts go through Moore city offices rather than through the larger city next door.

Sellers here tend to weigh a few recurring questions: whether storm damage has to be repaired first, whether an old shelter or addition was permitted, and how fast the sale can close. The sections below cover the city itself and then the local steps that affect a sale.

Where is Moore and how is the city laid out?

Moore sits in central Oklahoma, just south of Oklahoma City and north of Norman. According to the Census Bureau figures quoted on Wikipedia, the city covers 22.2 square miles, of which 21.8 square miles is land.

The size comes from a single decision. In 1961 Moore annexed 21.6 square miles, and it became a full city in 1962. Oklahoma City then grew from about 25 square miles to 643 square miles through annexation and ended up on the north, east and west sides of Moore, with Norman forming the southern border. A house in Moore can therefore be a few blocks from an Oklahoma City address and still sit under a different city code, a different permit office.

The ground is part of the Sandstone Hills region, which is known for hills with blackjack oak and post oak.

What is the short history of Moore?

Moore began as a railroad stop. Its post office opened on May 27, 1889, during the Land Run, and the town took the name of Al Moore, a Santa Fe railway employee who painted his name on a board and nailed it to the boxcar he lived in. The community incorporated in 1893.

For decades it stayed tiny. The 1960 census counted 1,221 people. The count was 35,063 in 1980 and 55,081 in 2010, so a large share of Moore's houses were probably built after the annexation.

How do tornadoes affect selling a house in Moore?

Tornado history is the first thing many Moore buyers ask about, and sellers should be ready with plain answers. The Oklahoma City metro sits in Tornado Alley, and the city has been damaged by significant tornadoes on October 4, 1998, May 3, 1999, May 8, 2003, May 10, 2010 and May 20, 2013, with weaker ones on May 31, 2013 and March 25, 2015.

The May 3, 1999 storm was rated F5 and left a damage path more than a mile wide at times. The May 20, 2013 storm was rated EF5, hit Briarwood and Plaza Towers elementary schools while classes were in session, and killed 24 people, according to the state medical examiner as reported by Wikipedia.

What that means for a sale in practical terms:

  • A storm shelter or safe room is a selling point, but only if it was permitted. Moore requires a permit for a shelter and its inspections division handles the application at City Hall.
  • At a May 2026 Building Safety Month event, city staff offered to verify whether a shelter is registered with emergency management, so ask the Inspections Division whether that check is available before you list.
  • Oklahoma's SoonerSafe program, run by the state emergency management office, has offered rebates for safe rooms through FEMA grants, so ask whether a rebate was ever claimed on the property.
  • Roof and window repairs after hail or wind are common. Keep invoices and permits together so a buyer can see what was done and when.

What permits and codes apply to a Moore house?

Moore requires a building permit for most remodels, additions and improvements, and for all new construction. If you are unsure, the Inspections Department asks people to call 405-793-5051.

Permits and inspections run through the city's GovBuilt portal. Same-day inspections are available when you call or message through the portal before 9 a.m. The city has adopted the 2018 International Residential Code, the 2018 International Property Maintenance Code and the 2020 National Electric Code, all as amended by the city and the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission.

Open or unpermitted work is where sales stall. A buyer's lender or inspector may ask for permit records on a garage conversion, a fence, a patio slab or a shelter poured into a garage floor. Code enforcement is a separate desk at the same address, reachable at 405-793-5052, and it handles weeds, debris and property maintenance complaints.

You can start at the City of Moore permits page.

What is the weather like in Moore, and what does it do to a house?

Moore has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers, and the weather source Wikipedia cites puts July's average daily high at about 93 degrees Fahrenheit. Annual precipitation in that data set is about 18 inches, with May the wettest month at 2.81 inches.

Wikipedia also notes that prolonged heavy rain often leads to flash flooding and that severe ice storms and snowstorms happen sporadically in winter. The metro area is subject to frequent hailstorms along with tornadoes. For a house, that points to a short list of things a buyer's inspector will look at first:

  • Roof age, shingle condition and hail marks
  • Window and garage door damage
  • Drainage around the foundation after heavy rain
  • Attic and ceiling stains from past leaks

Written repair records help. When a roof has been replaced after an insurance claim, the paperwork often matters more to a buyer than the roof itself.

Which schools serve Moore?

Moore Public Schools is the main district, and its own website describes it as the fourth-largest public school district in Oklahoma, with about 35 schools. The district boundaries cover more than the city limits, so confirm the district for a specific address instead of assuming it from the mailing city.

Because Moore borders Oklahoma City and Norman, some addresses with a Moore or nearby mailing name fall in other districts. Wikipedia's articles on Oklahoma City and Norman both list Moore Public Schools among the districts that cover parts of those cities. Buyers who care about schools usually check the district map before making an offer.

How are property taxes and closing handled for a Moore sale?

Moore is in Cleveland County, so the county assessor sets values and the county treasurer collects the bill. The county's treasurer information says taxes can be paid in two installments: if exactly half is paid by December 31, the second half is due by March 31, and if nothing is paid by December 31 the bill becomes delinquent.

Oklahoma also requires most sellers of one or two dwelling units to give the buyer a written condition disclosure or a disclaimer statement under the Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act, 60 O.S. section 831 and following. The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission publishes the form. A seller who fills it out honestly and discloses a known defect, such as past storm damage, limits later liability for that item under section 835.

Before you sign anything, ask the title company for a payoff figure, any open permits and the current tax status. That small checklist prevents most closing surprises.

What do sellers in Moore usually face?

Moore sellers most often deal with one of a handful of situations. Each has a different best route, and a cash sale is one option among them.

  • Storm or hail damage that has not been repaired and an insurance claim that is still open
  • An inherited house where the heirs live elsewhere and want a clean sale
  • Rental property with a tenant, deferred maintenance or a city code notice
  • A shelter, addition or garage conversion with no permit on file
  • A short timeline caused by a move, a job change or a mortgage problem

Cash buyers purchase houses as they are, so a leaking roof or an old kitchen does not have to be fixed first. The offer will reflect the condition, and you can compare it with what a repaired and listed sale would likely net after repairs, agent fees and time on market. Ask any buyer for the terms in writing and read them before deciding.

More questions about Moore, OK

Is Moore, Oklahoma part of Oklahoma City?

No. Moore is its own incorporated city in Cleveland County, even though Oklahoma City surrounds it on the north, east and west. Permits, code enforcement and city utilities for a Moore address go through the City of Moore.

Do I need a permit record to sell a house with a storm shelter in Moore?

Moore requires a permit for a storm shelter, and buyers or their lenders may ask for it. Call the Inspections Division at 405-793-5051 to confirm what is on file, and ask whether the shelter is registered with emergency management.

When are property taxes due in Cleveland County?

Cleveland County says taxes can be paid in full or in two halves. At least half must be paid by December 31 to avoid delinquency, and the second half is due by March 31.

Do I have to disclose tornado damage when I sell in Moore?

Oklahoma law asks sellers of one or two dwelling units to give the buyer a disclosure statement or a disclaimer statement. If you know about a defect, such as past storm damage, list it on the form. Ask a real estate attorney if you are unsure how to answer a question.

Can I sell a Moore house as-is for cash?

Yes, a cash buyer can purchase a house in its current condition, and sellers often choose this route when repairs, probate or timing make a listing hard. Compare any offer with your other options and get the terms in writing.

Landowner W. P. Atkinson bought land after hearing an air field might be built nearby. The field was later renamed Tinker Air Force Base for Major General Clarence L. How much does Tinker Air Force Base drive the Midwest City economy?

Tinker is the largest single-site employer in Oklahoma, with more than 26,000 military and civilian employees according to the base fact sheet. The base's FY 2025 economic impact statement lists 25,669 direct personnel and 32,816 indirect personnel, with a direct payroll near $1.98 billion.

Direct personnel fell about 4.8 percent from FY 2024 while indirect personnel rose about 11.4 percent. The Air Force says the Oklahoma City Air Logistics Complex alone employs more than 9,000 military and civilian professionals.

Midwest City also has a regional hospital, dedicated October 6, 1962, and aerospace businesses. The former General Motors Oklahoma City Assembly plant, open from 1979 until February 2006, is now part of the Tinker Aerospace Complex. A city this tied to one employer can see housing demand follow federal staffing and contract news.

  • Tinker: more than 26,000 employees, the largest single-site employer in the state
  • Midwest Regional Medical Center and other healthcare employers
  • Aerospace contractors tied to the Tinker Aerospace Complex
  • Rose State College and the school districts

What neighborhoods and landmarks define Midwest City?

Midwest City's growth came in waves. Voters approved a junior college district in 1968 and Oscar Rose Junior College, now Rose State College, opened in 1970. Heritage Park Mall opened in 1978, and Town Center Plaza and the Reed Center arrived after 2003. The city's Heritage Park Mall Urban Renewal Plan covers part of that area.

Wikipedia reports that in the early 1970s the Glenwood Addition subdivision was purchased and 835 homes were moved after aircraft crashes in the area. If your house is in an area with a history like this, expect questions and keep any records you have.

Population figures show how fast the city filled in: 10,166 residents in 1950, 36,058 in 1960 and 48,114 in 1970. The first Sam's Club opened here on April 7, 1983, and the 60,000-square-foot Reed Center added a convention venue in the 2000s. A house in an older section of that growth is likely to be decades old, so a buyer's inspector may look closely at its roof, plumbing and electrical systems.

What weather risks affect homes in Midwest City?

Midwest City has had direct tornado damage, in May 1999 and again on May 8, 2003. The 1999 storm killed 3 people and the 2003 storm injured 104, according to Wikipedia.

Average rainfall is about 35.9 inches a year, peaking in May at 5.44 inches, and daily highs average 93 degrees in July. Roofing, hail damage and storm shelters are routine conversation points for buyers in the metro. Gather claim letters and shelter documentation before you list.

Which school districts serve Midwest City?

Most Midwest City addresses are in the Mid-Del School District, which includes Midwest City High School, Carl Albert High School, Midwest City Middle School, Carl Albert Middle School and the Mid-Del Technology Center. Rose State College is in the city.

Parts of the city fall under other districts: Choctaw/Nicoma Park Schools, Oklahoma City Public Schools (with zoned schools such as Willow Brook Elementary, Spencer Elementary, Rogers Intermediate and Star Spencer Mid-High) and Crutcho Public School. Because the district can change from one block to the next, confirm it before you advertise a school.

What does Midwest City code enforcement look like?

The city has a Code Enforcement Division within its services, plus a Citizen Code Violation Lookup page and a page called Structures for Potential Investors. The Community Development department also handles permits and inspections, planning and zoning, and trade license renewals.

Permits matter at resale too. Buyers and their inspectors compare what is in the house with what the city has on file, so unpermitted additions, converted garages or replaced systems can slow a financed sale. A cash buyer can usually take those issues as they are, though the price reflects them.

The violation lookup is useful before you sell: search your address to see whether a case is open. If a buyer or title company finds an open case, closing can slow while it is cleared.

  • Search your address on the city's code violation lookup.
  • Resolve open cases before listing or disclose them clearly.
  • Ask Permits and Inspections whether work on the house was permitted.
  • Keep receipts for roof, electrical and plumbing work.

How do Oklahoma County property taxes work at a Midwest City sale?

The Oklahoma County Assessor values the property, and the County Treasurer collects the tax. The Treasurer's office is at 320 Robert S. Kerr Avenue, Suite 307, in Oklahoma City, and the phone number is 405-270-0082. Tax records can be searched through the Treasurer's Public Access page, and land records are searched through the County Clerk.

The Assessor's homestead notice says the exemption removes the first $1,000 of assessed value from taxation and limits assessment increases to 3 percent a year. You must live in the house on January 1 and apply by March 15. The 2025 notice also described an additional exemption for households with income of $30,000 or less and a senior valuation freeze for owners 65 and older earning $89,500 or less. Check current limits with the Assessor at 405-713-1236.

A mid-year sale means the tax is split between buyer and seller at closing, and the title company handles the math.

What are your options for selling a Midwest City house quickly?

You can list, sell privately or take a direct cash offer. Listing fits a house in good shape and a seller who can wait. A cash sale fits an inherited house, a rental with tenants, a house with deferred repairs or a tight timeline.

Oklahoma law requires a disclaimer or disclosure statement to reach the buyer before an offer is accepted (60 O.S. section 833). Gather your tax statement, any permits and the code lookup result, then call us with the Midwest City address and we will explain the offer. You can say no.

More questions about Midwest City, OK

What is the biggest employer in Midwest City?

Tinker Air Force Base, which gave the city its name through the Midwest Air Depot, is the largest single-site employer in Oklahoma, with more than 26,000 military and civilian employees according to the base.

Which school district covers Midwest City?

Most addresses are in the Mid-Del School District. Other parts are served by Choctaw/Nicoma Park, Oklahoma City Public Schools or Crutcho, so check the specific address.

Does Midwest City have a code violation lookup?

Yes. The city's Code Enforcement page links a Citizen Code Violation Lookup, which you can use to check for open cases on a property before you sell.

How does the Oklahoma County homestead exemption work?

It removes the first $1,000 of assessed value from tax and limits assessment increases to 3 percent a year. You must live in the home on January 1 and apply by March 15.

Has Midwest City been hit by tornadoes?

Yes. Wikipedia notes tornado damage in May 1999 and on May 8, 2003. Keep roof and storm damage paperwork ready for buyers.

Where is Enid and how is the city laid out?

Enid sits in northwestern Oklahoma at the eastern edge of the Great Plains, about 70 miles north of Oklahoma City. It is the county seat of Garfield County and covers roughly 74 square miles at an elevation near 1,250 feet.

Several federal and state routes cross the city: U.S. 81, U.S. 412, U.S. 64, U.S. 60 and State Highway 45. Older sections of town carry names that sellers will recognize from listings and tax bills, including Kenwood, Waverley, Weatherly, East Hill, Kinser Heights, Buena Vista, McKinley, Southern Heights and East Park.

The layout matters for a sale because Enid is large and flat, so the same street can mix 1900s homes, mid-century ranches and newer builds. Two houses a few blocks apart can have different school districts, different tax rates and, in the historic districts, different rules about what you may change or tear down.

What is Enid's history, and why does it matter for older houses?

Enid was founded during the Cherokee Outlet land run of 1893, and it was named for a character in Tennyson's Idylls of the King. The land office for the run was in Enid, and the town plat is said to have filled with about 12,000 people on the afternoon of the run.

That early start left a stock of pre-1940 homes close to downtown. The city adopted design guidelines for the Kenwood and Waverley Historic District, and its Historic Preservation Ordinance sets the criteria for applications to demolish historic structures. If your house is inside that district, ask the city's community development office before you promise a buyer a teardown or a major exterior change.

Enid has also been tied to the grain trade for most of its life. It is nicknamed the Wheat Capital of Oklahoma for its grain storage capacity, and mills and elevators from companies such as Pillsbury and General Mills operated there. Many older homes were built for workers connected to that industry and the railroads that served it.

What does Enid's economy look like for a home seller?

Enid's two best-known anchors are grain storage and Vance Air Force Base. Vance, a pilot training base, is a large local employer, and the city's own Vance partnership page reports more than 2,600 military and civilian personnel working there and more than 410 pilots trained each year for the Air Force, Navy, Marines and allied nations.

The Air Force's FY 2022 economic impact statement for Vance lists 2,571 personnel, a payroll of about $311 million and a total annual impact of about $739 million. The city's own page cites $220 million for local impact, so treat both as estimates that measure different things.

Other named employers include AdvancePierre Foods, Atwood Distributing, Johnston Enterprises, Pumpstar, Groendyke Transport and a Koch Industries plant that makes anhydrous ammonia. Higher education adds Northern Oklahoma College, Northwestern Oklahoma State University and the Autry Technology Center.

  • Student pilots and rotating staff mean some owners leave on a military timetable, not a listing timetable.
  • A house with deferred repairs competes against a large supply of older homes, so condition drives the buyer pool.

How does Enid's weather affect a house?

Enid has hot summers, cold and snowy winters and spring thunderstorms that can produce tornadoes. Temperatures have fallen below 0 degrees Fahrenheit in winter and risen above 100 in summer, with a recorded high of 118 in 1936 and a low of minus 20 in 1905.

Heavy rain is part of the record too: Enid holds Oklahoma's greatest one-day rainfall total from an official gauge, 15.68 inches on October 11, 1973. Roofs, gutters and foundations are where a buyer's inspector will look first.

If you are selling a house with storm damage, keep any insurance claim paperwork and contractor estimates together. A buyer will ask whether a claim was paid and whether the repair was finished. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands, which spares you from fixing a roof you are about to leave behind.

Which school districts serve Enid addresses?

Seven public districts serve the Enid area: Enid Public Schools, Chisholm, Kremlin-Hillsdale, Pioneer-Pleasant Vale, Waukomis, Drummond and Garber. Which one applies depends on the exact address, not on the mailing city.

This matters for taxes. The county assessor says millage in Garfield County varies by school district, municipality and technology center district, and rates run from $74.65 per $1,000 of assessed value in the lowest district to $102.02 in Drummond. The assessor also says Enid Public Schools typically has the lowest mill levy of any 6A school district in the state. Check the district on a buyer's tax bill before you quote a monthly cost.

What property rules can catch Enid sellers off guard?

The most common surprises are overgrown lots and structures the city considers dilapidated. In Enid, grass or weeds taller than 12 inches is a violation. The city posts a notice on the property and sends a certified letter, and you have 10 days to fix it before the city can mow and clean the lot and charge the cost to the property.

Dilapidated and unsecured buildings follow a longer path. The owner meets a hearing officer, who sets a deadline that may be 10 days or up to 30 days or more depending on the arrangement. If the work is not done, the city may remove the building or board it up and assess the cost against the property. A recent Enid commission packet shows the city filing a notice of dilapidation and lien under Title 11 of the Oklahoma Statutes.

  • Cut and clear the lot before photos or showings.
  • Secure broken windows and open doors on vacant houses.
  • Call code staff at 580-616-7213 to ask about open cases on the address.
  • Pay or resolve any city charge before closing so it does not become a lien the buyer has to clear.

When are Garfield County property taxes due, and how do they work at a sale?

Garfield County mails tax bills in November. You can pay in halves: half by December 31 and the rest by March 31, and if nothing is paid by December 31 the full amount becomes delinquent on January 1.

The assessor values property as of January 1 at fair cash value and applies a 12.5 percent ratio. As its own example, a $100,000 home with a $102.02 millage rate and the homestead exemption comes to about $1,173 in tax. Homestead applications are due by March 15 for the current year. The assessor sends change of valuation notices in the first week of March and the protest period ends on the first Monday in April, or 30 days from the date on a valuation notice.

The Garfield County Treasurer (580-237-0246) handles payment and tax roll searches. At closing, the title company normally checks the treasurer's records and settles any unpaid balance, so it is worth looking up your parcel before you list.

What does a seller have to disclose in Oklahoma?

An Oklahoma seller must give the buyer either a property disclaimer statement or a property condition disclosure statement. State law says this should happen as soon as practicable and before the buyer's offer is accepted, and a buyer can sue if it is not delivered in time. The statutes are 60 O.S. sections 831 to 839 on the Oklahoma Legislature site.

If you list the house, disclosures, repairs requested after inspection and agent commissions all shape what you keep. If you sell to a company that buys houses for cash, the sale usually goes by contract between you and the buyer, and the disclosure still applies.

How can you sell a house in Enid quickly?

You have three routes: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a direct cash offer. A traditional listing suits a house that shows well and can wait for a financed buyer. A direct cash sale suits houses with repair needs, probate, tenants, back taxes or a firm move date.

Enid's older housing stock and its mix of military and agricultural households mean timing varies a lot between owners. If a lender is already involved, ask for a payoff figure first. If the house came through an estate, ask the county court clerk whether the file is closed. Our team can talk through the Enid address and explain what a cash offer would and would not cover, with no obligation to accept it.

Is Enid in a county that charges a different property tax rate than nearby towns?

Yes, millage rates differ by school district and municipality within Garfield County. The Garfield County Assessor reports a range from $74.65 to $102.02 per $1,000 of assessed value, depending on where the property sits.

How long do I have to cut weeds on an Enid property after a notice?

You have 10 days. Enid treats grass or weeds over 12 inches as a violation, posts a sign and sends a certified letter. After 10 days the city can mow the lot and assess the cost against the property.

Does Vance Air Force Base affect who buys houses in Enid?

It can. The base employs more than 2,600 people according to the city, and some of them rent or buy locally for a limited number of years. Sellers close to the base may see more military buyers and more owners who relocate on orders.

What happens if my Enid house is declared dilapidated?

You are given a hearing with a hearing officer, who sets a correction deadline. If the work is not done, the city can remove or board up the building and assess the cost against the property, which can create a lien that has to be cleared at sale.

When is the Garfield County homestead exemption deadline?

March 15. Applications can be filed during the year but must be in by March 15 to count for the current tax year. Contact the Garfield County Assessor at 580-237-0220 to confirm the current forms.

Where is Bartlesville and what shapes the housing here?

Bartlesville sits in Washington County in northeastern Oklahoma, with a small part of the city extending into Osage County. The Caney River runs through town and separates downtown from the east side.

The 2020 census counted 37,290 residents and 17,140 housing units, and 11.7% of those units were vacant. Among occupied homes, 66.3% were owner-occupied and 33.7% were rented. For a seller, that mix means a fair number of buyers are investors or landlords as well as owner-occupants.

The city covers about 21 square miles and is largely built out. The town was incorporated in 1897 and platted in 1898, so many of the older neighborhoods around downtown carry houses that are a century old or close to it. Those homes often come with original plumbing, wiring and foundations that a buyer's inspector will look at closely.

What is Bartlesville's economy built on?

Oil built Bartlesville, and energy companies still anchor the job market. Oklahoma's first commercial oil well, the Nellie Johnstone No. 1, came in along the Caney River on April 15, 1897, and Frank and L.E. Phillips founded Phillips Petroleum here in 1917.

Phillips Petroleum later merged into ConocoPhillips, and the company spun off Phillips 66 in 2012. The two companies together employ or contract with more than 3,800 people in the area,, and Chevron Phillips also keeps an office in town.

Other employers and institutions shape demand for housing too:

  • Two industrial parks, the Bartlesville Industrial Park and the Sunset Industrial Park, where a lithium-ion battery recycling plant landed in September 2023.
  • Oklahoma Wesleyan University, with about 1,100 students, and a Rogers State University branch campus downtown with about 700.
  • Tri County Technology Center, which runs career training for high school and adult students.

What does Bartlesville weather mean for a house?

Bartlesville has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers, cool winters and most of its rain in spring. It sits in Tornado Alley, so severe weather is most common from April through June.

That swing from triple digits to deep cold is hard on roofs, HVAC equipment and exposed plumbing. A buyer who sees stained ceilings, a patched roof or an old furnace will price the repair in, and a cash buyer usually does the same arithmetic before making an offer.

How have floods and tornadoes affected Bartlesville properties?

Two floods and one major tornado are part of the city's recent record, and each can show up in buyer questions. The Caney River flooded in October 1986 after unusually heavy rain, splitting the city in half for several days. It broke its banks again in June 2007 and crested five feet below the 1986 level.

An EF4 tornado struck Bartlesville and nearby Barnsdall on May 6, 2024, and debris cleanup was still under way in July 2024. Buyers often ask whether storm repairs were permitted and finished.

The city also warns that some properties lie in floodplains or floodways. Development there can be regulated or prohibited, and a floodplain development permit may be required before you add to or alter a structure. If your house is near the river, expect a buyer to ask about flood zone status and insurance before they sign.

Which Bartlesville city rules matter before you sell?

The city's Building and Construction Services division handles permits, and its page advises calling 918.338.4244 before any project to confirm whether a permit applies. Unpermitted work is a common source of delays at closing, so it is worth checking before you list or accept an offer.

According to the division, permits are required for:

  • Structural construction, alteration, demolition or remodel, including re-roofing that changes the roof structure.
  • Fences over seven feet and walls over four feet.
  • Electrical work, including solar and generator installs.
  • Mechanical work such as furnaces, water heaters and fuel-gas piping.
  • Plumbing, with limited exceptions for faucet repairs and clearing stoppages.
  • Pools or hot tubs 24 inches or deeper.

Painting, tile, carpet, cabinets and like-for-like replacement of doors and windows do not need a building permit. The city enforces the state's minimum construction codes, adopted by the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission.

How does Bartlesville enforce property maintenance?

The Neighborhood Services Division enforces the city's minimum property maintenance codes and typically acts on complaints rather than patrolling. Its page lists the most common violations as tall grass and weeds, junk and trash, deteriorated fences and structures, broken windows, parking on grass, inoperable vehicles, improperly stored recreational vehicles and illegal signs.

The division reports that more than 2,000 complaints are filed and investigated in a year, and about 97 percent are resolved through voluntary compliance. Complaints can be filed online, at City Hall, 401 S. Johnstone Ave., or by phone at 918.338.4230.

Owners of vacant or deteriorated buildings should know about the Voluntary Demolition Program. It lets owners demolish dilapidated structures at a reduced fee and avoid nuisance actions, though participation is voluntary and funding is limited. A neglected inherited house with open code complaints is a typical reason owners here look at a direct sale.

How does property tax work for a Bartlesville home in Washington County?

The Washington County Assessor values every property as of January 1 each year, and the county treasurer bills the tax. The assessor's office says it runs a four-year revaluation cycle, so each property is visually inspected at least once in that period.

If you disagree with the value, start with an informal protest by visiting the assessor, who arranges a follow-up inspection. You can then file a written protest with the county Board of Equalization, an independent three-member board. If that fails, you may appeal to district court within twenty days after the Board adjourns or twenty days after May 31, whichever is later.

The county says the assessor sets value, not the tax rate. Schools, cities and townships set levies after public hearings. Contact the assessor at (918) 337-2830 or the treasurer at 918-337-2810. Homestead status matters when you sell: the assessor asks owners to report it if they sell or stop living in the house as their primary residence.

What paperwork does an Oklahoma seller in Bartlesville handle at closing?

Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax on deeds at 75 cents for each $500 of consideration, collected by the county clerk when the deed is recorded. On a $150,000 sale, that is 300 units of $500, or $225.

The statute says the tax is paid by anyone who makes, signs, issues or sells the instrument, and the Oklahoma Tax Commission notes both grantor and grantee can be held responsible. Your purchase contract decides who pays in practice, and the Washington County Clerk records the deed.

Oklahoma law also requires sellers of one or two residential units to give the buyer either a property condition disclosure statement or a disclaimer statement under 60 O.S. section 833. Sellers who choose a disclosure should fill it out honestly, because the form covers roof, plumbing, electrical and other systems.

Which schools and roads serve Bartlesville?

Almost all of the Washington County part of Bartlesville falls in Bartlesville Public Schools, Independent School District 30, which runs six elementary sites, Central and Madison middle schools and the high school. A few northern parts fall in Dewey Public Schools, and some Osage County sections are covered by Dewey and Osage Hills.

US-75 runs north and south, US-60 runs east and west, and State Highway 123 also serves the city. Tulsa International Airport is about 45 miles south, and Bartlesville Municipal Airport, a city-owned single-runway field, handles general aviation. Buyers commuting to Tulsa often ask about drive time, so mention it in any listing or offer conversation.

More questions about Bartlesville, OK

Can I sell a house in Bartlesville with code violations?

Yes. Open code complaints do not prevent a sale, but they must be dealt with or disclosed, and a buyer will price them in. Contact Neighborhood Services at 918.338.4230 to learn what is open on your property.

Do I need a permit to repair a roof in Bartlesville?

It depends on the work. The city says re-roofing that changes the roof structure or framework needs a building permit, and the division suggests calling 918.338.4244 to confirm before starting.

Does Washington County send a notice when my home value changes?

Oklahoma assessors value property as of January 1 each year. The county describes an informal protest, then a Board of Equalization appeal, then district court, so keep any valuation notice and call (918) 337-2830 promptly with questions.

Is Bartlesville in a flood zone?

Parts of it are. The city notes some properties lie in floodplains or floodways, and the Caney River flooded the city in 1986 and 2007. Check your parcel with the city's engineering department before you list.

What should a Muskogee homeowner know before selling?

Selling a house in Muskogee means dealing with a smaller city that has a long industrial history, a strict nuisance-abatement process and an unusual tax question that came up in 2026. Owners can list, sell privately or take a cash offer, and in Muskogee the condition of the house and the city's code rules often decide which route makes sense.

This page covers the city, its economy and weather, the local code and tax issues, and the steps at closing.

Where is Muskogee and what is its geography?

Muskogee is the county seat of Muskogee County in eastern Oklahoma, about 50 miles southeast of Tulsa. The Census Bureau lists 44.5 square miles of total area, of which 43.0 is land.

The Arkansas, Verdigris and Grand rivers meet in the northeast corner of the city, an area historically called Three Rivers. Elevation is low for Oklahoma, around 600 feet, and the city sits on the line between the eastern oak and hickory forest and the prairie of the Great Plains. Low ground and river valleys are worth checking on a flood map before a house goes on the market.
