How did Muskogee grow?

The first permanent settlement near Muskogee dates to 1817 on the south bank of the Verdigris River. After the Indian Removal Act of 1830 the Muscogee (Creek) Nation was relocated here, and the Indian Agency building on Agency Hill, now inside Honor Heights Park, hosted meetings of the Five Civilized Tribes.

The Missouri, Kansas and Texas Railroad reached the area in 1872, a federal court opened in Muskogee in 1889, and the city incorporated in 1898. Businessman Charles N. Haskell, who later became Oklahoma's first governor, moved in during 1901 and helped build railroads and a five-story business block. Muskogee's population passed 25,000 by 1910. In 1905 delegates met here to draft a constitution for a proposed State of Sequoyah, which was never authorized.

What is Muskogee's economy based on?

Muskogee is an economic center for eastern Oklahoma with a manufacturing base. Georgia-Pacific operates a tissue and paper towel plant of 2.9 million square feet, listed as the city's largest employer with about 800 workers.

Two newer announcements are worth watching:

  • Stardust Power broke ground on January 22, 2025 for a lithium refinery near the Port of Muskogee, described as a $1.2 billion project with an initial capacity of 25,000 metric tons a year.
  • On November 20, 2025 Google announced two data centers in the Muskogee area, one near Summit about 7 miles south and one near Council Hill about 25 miles southeast.

The Port of Muskogee sits on the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System, and Union Pacific and BNSF serve the city by rail. Higher education includes Northeastern State University, Connors State College and Indian Capital Technology Center. The effect on housing demand is not something we can promise, so treat these projects as context, not a forecast.

How does Muskogee code enforcement affect a house sale?

Muskogee Code Enforcement responds to complaints about nuisance, zoning and property maintenance violations. The most common are high weeds and grass, trash and debris, vehicles parked on the grass, people living in an RV outside an RV park, inoperable vehicles and derelict structures.

The city says complaints are anonymous and that the legal process takes time, asking residents to allow 15 to 20 business days for results. The number is (918) 684-6235. Sellers of vacant or neglected houses should clear yard violations before showings, because an open notice can come up in a buyer's search of city records.

The city's code of ordinances also states that vacant, abandoned or dilapidated structures create blight and lower property values. A house in that condition may be a candidate for condemnation, so heirs and out-of-town owners should check their status early. You can read the city's code enforcement page for current details.

What is the $29.25 million judgment issue and how could it affect property taxes?

In a September 1, 2026 letter, City Manager Kendal Francis said three inverse condemnation cases against the city, filed in 2007, resulted in judgments totaling $29.25 million plus interest. The cases were England ($8.5 million), Taff ($6.5 million) and Lacey ($14.25 million), and they arose from properties condemned and demolished under the city's nuisance abatement process about twenty years ago. The council approved settlement agreements on August 24, 2026.

The letter explains that Oklahoma cities use a sinking fund, paid by property tax, to cover court judgments. If the full amount were placed on it, the impact would be roughly $450 a year per $100,000 of property valuation, based on information from the Muskogee County Assessor. The decision would not need to be made until June 2027, any increase would begin in October 2027, and it would stay on the tax rolls for three years. The council said it is exploring other ways to pay.

No final decision had been announced in that letter, so sellers should treat this as a possibility, not a set bill. A buyer comparing taxes may ask about it, and the letter is public on the city website.

How are Muskogee property taxes calculated?

The Muskogee County Assessor explains the formula in a one-page guide. The assessor sets fair cash value, the Oklahoma constitution requires real property to be assessed at no less than 11 percent and no more than 13.5 percent of that value, and the result is multiplied by the millage rate of the taxing districts.

The guide's worked example uses a $300,000 house: $300,000 times 11 percent is $33,000, and at 102.39 mills the bill is $3,379. It says about 24 school districts operate in the county, with rates ranging from 76.22 mills in Wainwright to 105.49 in Hilldale, which works out to $2,515 versus $3,481 on the same example. Hilldale Public Schools covers a small southern part of Muskogee, so where a house sits can change the bill.

As in the rest of Oklahoma, county information says tax is payable in two halves, with the first half due by December 31 and the second by March 31, so a closing in early year usually involves a tax proration or a payoff from the seller's proceeds.

Which schools serve Muskogee, and how do you get around?

Muskogee Public Schools covers most of the city limits and a large part of the county. Hilldale Public Schools serves a small southern portion and Fort Gibson Public Schools includes some areas in the east.

Roads include U.S. 62, 64 and 69 and State Highways 16 and 165, plus the Muskogee Turnpike. Davis Regional Airport is five miles south of downtown and has a 7,202-foot runway, while commercial flights use Tulsa International about 49 miles northwest.

What is the weather in Muskogee?

Muskogee is warmer and more humid than much of Oklahoma. The record high is 118 degrees Fahrenheit, set August 10, 1936, and the record low is minus 14 on February 13, 1905. Average annual precipitation in the 1991 to 2020 normals is about 43 inches, with May the wettest month at 5.25 inches.

Heat, humidity and rain are hard on roofs, crawl spaces and older siding, so buyers often ask about moisture history. A recent roof or documented drainage fix helps a listing or a cash conversation.

What do Muskogee sellers usually run into?

  • Vacant or inherited houses with overgrown lots or open code notices
  • Older homes that need roof, foundation or plumbing work
  • Rental properties where tenants have left the property in poor condition
  • Owners worried about the possible tax increase
  • Sellers who live out of town and cannot manage repairs

A cash buyer will usually buy a house as it is, including those with code issues, but the price will reflect repairs and risk. Ask for the offer in writing and compare it with the net from a repaired and listed sale.

More questions about Muskogee, OK

How long does Muskogee code enforcement take to resolve a complaint?

The city asks residents to allow 15 to 20 business days because it has a legal process to follow. Complaints can be made by phone at (918) 684-6235 and are kept anonymous.

Could Muskogee property taxes go up because of the court judgments?

Possibly. The city manager's September 1, 2026 letter said the judgments total $29.25 million and could add about $450 a year per $100,000 of valuation if placed on the sinking fund. The decision would come in June 2027 and any increase would start in October 2027 and last three years.

What percent of value is real property assessed at in Oklahoma?

The state constitution sets the assessment ratio between 11 and 13.5 percent of fair cash value, according to the Muskogee County Assessor. The result is multiplied by the millage rate.

When are property taxes due in Muskogee County?

Under the standard Oklahoma schedule described by county treasurers, at least half is due by December 31 and the second half by March 31. Call the county treasurer at (918) 682-0811 to confirm a current balance.

Can I sell a Muskogee house that has a code violation?

Yes, many buyers will purchase a house with open violations, but the notice may need to be resolved or disclosed at closing. Ask the city for the status and get any cash offer in writing.

Where is Bixby and how is the city laid out?

Bixby is a suburb south of Tulsa, and the Arkansas River splits it into a north and a south half. The original town center sits south of the river, and the city lies in both Tulsa and Wagoner counties.

Alexander Posey, a member of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, settled the area in the late 1800s, and the town took its name from Tams Bixby, a chairman of the Dawes Commission. The original 80-acre townsite plat was approved in 1902, and Bixby incorporated in 1906 with 400 residents. A railroad depot built about half a mile north in 1904 briefly split the community into two towns, with streets deliberately surveyed so they did not line up.

That patchwork shows today: older homes near the original streets, newer subdivisions spread across the former farmland. A seller should know which part of town the house is in, because river-side and creek-side lots raise different buyer questions than hilltop or interior ones.

How fast has Bixby grown, and who lives in its houses?

What is Bixby's farming heritage, and does it still matter?

Bixby calls itself The Garden Spot of Oklahoma, a nickname it received in 1941 when the town was a regional shipping point for produce. Farmers first grew cotton, wheat and alfalfa in the river bottom, then switched to truck farming of vegetables in the 1930s.

Most of those truck farms later became sod fields, typically Bermuda grass, or were developed for homes and businesses. Only a small share of residents now work in agriculture, but the city still holds its Green Corn Festival each June.

Gas deposits discovered in 1905 and 1906 and oil fields in 1913 also touched the local economy. For sellers, the useful takeaway is that much of today's housing sits on former farm and river-bottom ground, so soil movement, grading and drainage are fair inspection topics.

What flood and drainage issues come up in Bixby?

Flooding along the Arkansas River and its creeks has been a real planning issue. The city's August 2020 Beacon newsletter said the Haikey Creek levee would bring 920 acres out of the floodplain, addressing one of the last major flood-impaired areas north of the river.

The Oklahoma Water Resources Board lists a floodplain administrator for Bixby, and Oklahoma senators have publicly pushed for funding to repair Arkansas River levee systems that were described as at high risk of failure. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance depending on the map, so check the current flood zone before you set a price.

  • Gather any elevation certificate or past flood insurance claims.
  • Be ready to answer drainage questions about the lot, not only the house.

The City of Bixby's Public Works Authority is the local water supplier, and the water itself comes from the City of Tulsa through connections on all sides of town. Bixby's utility service guide also lists providers for sewer, natural gas, telecommunications, electricity and trash, and notes that trash service reaches residents north and south of the river and nearby communities such as Leonard and Liberty.

Bixby Telephone Company, known as BTC Broadband, has offered internet service since 1993 and has installed fiber in select neighborhoods. Confirm which providers serve the specific address, since the city's guide indicates availability can differ north and south of the Arkansas River.

If you are moving out, schedule a final water reading and transfer or stop service on the closing date so the buyer does not inherit your charges.

Bixby handles code enforcement through its police department, and the city's page explains what does and does not count as a nuisance. For example, a single blade of grass taller than 12 inches is not a violation; the tall growth must cover the majority of the yard as estimated by code enforcement.

Homeowners association covenants are a separate matter from city code. A buyer's agent will often ask about HOA dues and restrictions, so collect your HOA documents early.

The city's Development Services department runs the building permit process and requires electrical, plumbing and mechanical work to be done by contractors licensed with the city, according to its construction guidelines. If you finished a basement, built a deck or replaced a water heater, locate the permit and final inspection records. A cash buyer will usually take a house as is, but missing paperwork is easier to resolve before you sign.

How are Bixby property taxes assessed in Tulsa County?

Most of Bixby is assessed by the Tulsa County Assessor, which values property as of January 1 each year. The assessor's own FAQ explains that assessed value is currently 11 percent of the taxable fair cash value.

Taxable value for homesteads cannot rise more than 3 percent a year, and for other real property the cap is 5 percent. Those caps lift when title transfers, so the buyer's first tax bill can be higher than yours. That is a regular surprise for buyers who rely on the seller's number.

Under 68 O.S. section 3201, the state taxes a conveyed deed at 75 cents per $500 of price. On a $275,000 sale that means 550 units and $412.50, paid through the county clerk at recording.

Oklahoma also requires one- and two-unit sellers to hand the buyer either a condition disclosure or a disclaimer statement, as set out in 60 O.S. section 833 and the Real Estate Commission's forms. Whichever you choose, deliver it in writing.

Bixby Public Schools serves the town. Buyers with children often ask about attendance zones, and part of Broken Arrow also falls in the Bixby district, so confirm the exact boundary for your address.

The statute reaches anyone who signs or sells the deed, and the Tax Commission says both parties can be held responsible. Your contract states who pays at closing.

You have 30 calendar days from the date on the Notice of Valuation to file a written protest with the Tulsa County Assessor. Call (918) 596-5100 for help.

Where is Jenks, and what sets it apart from the rest of the Tulsa area?

Jenks is a Tulsa County suburb of Tulsa, set between the Arkansas River and U.S. Route 75 in northeastern Oklahoma. The city covers about 18 square miles at an elevation near 617 feet, and the Census Bureau estimate already on this page puts the population at 28,175 for July 2025.

Much of the city's identity comes from the river. The Riverwalk Crossing pedestrian bridge links the Jenks Riverwalk to the South Tulsa River Parks. The Oklahoma Aquarium is in Jenks, and the downtown area carries the nickname Antique Capital of Oklahoma.

For a seller, the practical point is that Jenks sits in the Tulsa metro but has its own city hall, permit office and ordinances, so local rules apply even when a buyer is shopping the whole region.

How did Jenks grow, and why does flood history matter?

Jenks began in 1904 as a community site on the Midland Valley Railroad between Tulsa and Muskogee, and it was named for the railroad's owner and director, William Henry Jenks. The town was platted in July 1905, the same year the Glenn Pool oil discovery brought business people and oil depots to the area.

When oil production slowed, farming took over again. Bulgarian families who immigrated in the 1920s set up vegetable farms. Floods from the Arkansas River and Polecat Creek struck repeatedly from 1904 through the 1950s, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built a levee around Jenks in 1948. Another severe flood threat arrived in 1986, when releases from Keystone Dam reached up to 300,000 cubic feet per second.

Anyone selling near the river or a creek should expect buyers and lenders to ask about floodplain status. The city requires a floodplain development permit for work in mapped floodplain areas, and its residential building permit form asks whether the property is located in a floodplain. Pull your elevation certificate or flood insurance paperwork if you have it, since it answers the question before it is asked.

What does the Jenks economy look like?

Jenks has a mix of manufacturing, utilities, finance and tourism. Kimberly-Clark built a manufacturing facility in the 1980s, and Public Service Company of Oklahoma, Green Country Energy, Tulsa Winch, Continental Wire Cloth and First Oklahoma Bank are listed as companies headquartered or based in the city.

The Richard Lloyd Jones Jr. Airport opened just outside Jenks in 1958 and spurred growth. The Tulsa water system and a gas-fired power plant expanded into Jenks in the 1970s. A citizen-led effort began in 2024 to restore abandoned infrastructure in an area called The Ten District.

  • Population grew from 16,924 in 2010 to 25,949 in 2020, a gain of roughly 9,000 residents in ten years.
  • The river crossing was rebuilt as the town grew: a single-lane bridge in 1910, a two-lane bridge in 1948 and a four-lane bridge in 1996.
  • The current high school building dates to 1960 and 1961.

Which schools serve Jenks addresses?

Jenks Public Schools is the main district, and it received the 2005 Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award. It is one of the largest districts in the state, and many of its schools stand inside the City of Tulsa, so a Jenks school zone does not always mean a Jenks mailing address.

Parts of the area are also served by Bixby Public Schools and Glenpool Public Schools. Confirm the district for a specific address with the school office before you advertise it, so a buyer does not rely on the wrong assumption.

What weather and safety issues should Jenks sellers know about?

Jenks regulates storm shelters through its permit office. A permit is needed for outdoor storm shelters, in-ground safe rooms and above-ground safe rooms built on site. Prefabricated above-ground safe rooms are exempt. Shelters must meet FEMA P-320 or ICC-500 standards and must sit in the rear yard outside setbacks and easements.

If you installed a shelter, find the permit and the manufacturer paperwork before you list. A permitted, standards-compliant shelter is a documented feature a buyer can verify. An unpermitted one can raise questions at inspection.

Permit applications are picked up at City Hall, second floor, 211 N Elm Street, or printed from the city's Protective Inspections page, and the city says processing takes at least three working days.

How are Tulsa County property taxes handled when a Jenks house sells?

The Tulsa County Assessor values property as of January 1 each year and mails a notice whenever the fair cash value increases. A taxpayer then has 30 calendar days from the date of the notice to protest in writing, or can protest by the first Monday in April even without an increase.

The Treasurer says at least half of the tax must be paid before January 1, and the second half before April 1. If half is not paid before January 1, the whole amount becomes due and is treated as delinquent.

One detail matters to your buyer. The assessor states that when a home is purchased, the statutory cap on its taxable value is removed, and properties are revalued every year. A buyer's tax bill can therefore differ from yours, which is worth saying early if the buyer is budgeting. Homestead applications must reach the assessor by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation notice.

What should you do before listing or selling a Jenks house?

Start with paperwork, then condition. Gather the tax statement, any floodplain or shelter permits, and the Oklahoma disclosure form. State law requires a seller to deliver a disclaimer or disclosure statement before the buyer's offer is accepted, and a buyer may sue if it is missing. The statute is 60 O.S. section 833 and the sections near it.

Then decide how fast you need to move. A listing can bring a financed buyer, but it comes with showings, inspections and a buyer's lender timeline. A direct cash sale shortens the path and takes the house in the condition it is in. If the property sits in a mapped flood area, has an unpermitted addition or has unpaid tax, tell us up front so the offer reflects the real situation.

Our editorial team writes these guides to explain choices, and any offer for a Jenks house is for you to accept or decline.

More questions about Jenks, OK

Is Jenks part of Tulsa?

No. Jenks is its own city in Tulsa County and a suburb of Tulsa. Many Jenks school buildings are physically inside Tulsa, which is why the school district and the mailing city can differ.

Do I need a permit for a storm shelter in Jenks?

Yes for outdoor shelters, in-ground safe rooms and on-site built above-ground safe rooms. Prefabricated above-ground safe rooms do not need one. The shelter must meet FEMA P-320 or ICC-500 and the city says processing takes at least three working days.

Does Jenks have flood risk?

The city has a floodplain development permit process, and local history includes repeated floods before a levee was built in 1948 and a flood threat in 1986. Check the floodplain status of your parcel with the city engineering office at 918-299-5883.

What happens to my property tax cap when I sell a Jenks home?

The Tulsa County Assessor says the cap on taxable value is removed when a home is purchased. The buyer's first bill can be higher than yours, so share your tax statement but tell the buyer to confirm with the assessor.

When are Tulsa County taxes due?

At least half before January 1 and the second half before April 1, according to the County Treasurer. Missing the first-half deadline makes the full amount due and subject to delinquent tax rules.
